title: Virtual Environments: Your Safe Sandbox 🏖️
description: Create isolated Python worlds so your experiments never break your system.

slides.title: The One Rule of Hacking Labs 🧪
slides.content:
# Never Mess Up Your Main System

Imagine you install a shady library to crack a WiFi password. It breaks your system Python, and now every Python app on your computer crashes. **Nightmare!**

That's why we use **virtual environments** – clean, separate Python installations that keep your experiments contained.

Think of them as disposable labs: if something explodes, just delete the lab and make a new one.

quizData.question: Why use a virtual environment for hacking projects?

options.text: It makes your code run faster
It isolates dependencies and prevents system‑wide breakage
It's required by law for ethical hacking

quizData.explanation: Virtual environments create a sandbox so libraries you install don't conflict with other projects or your OS.

slides.title: What Exactly is a Virtual Environment?
slides.content:
# A Folder with Its Own Python

A virtual environment (venv) is just a directory that contains:
* A copy of the Python interpreter
* Its own `pip` (package installer)
* Its own `site-packages` folder for libraries

When you **activate** it, your terminal points to that copy. Any packages you install go there, not to the global system. **Deactivate** to return to normal.

slides.title: Creating Your First Venv
slides.content: Navigate to your projects folder and run:
slides.codeSnippet:
# Windows (Command Prompt or PowerShell)
python -m venv hacklab

# macOS / Linux
python3 -m venv hacklab

slides.title: Inside the `hacklab` Folder
slides.content:
# What Was Just Created?

You'll see a folder called `hacklab` with:
* `hacklab/bin/` (or `Scripts/` on Windows) – contains the python executable and activation scripts
* `hacklab/lib/` – where installed packages live
* `hacklab/pyvenv.cfg` – a config file

**Never edit these files manually.** Just use activation commands.

quizData.question: After creating a virtual environment, you can directly use `python` from it without activation.
quizData.explanation: You must run the activation script first. Without it, your terminal still uses the global Python.

slides.title: Activation – The Magic Spell ✨
slides.content:
# Open a Terminal and Run:

**Windows (Command Prompt):**
```
hacklab\Scripts\activate
```
**Windows (PowerShell):**
```
hacklab\Scripts\Activate.ps1
```
**macOS / Linux:**
```
source hacklab/bin/activate
```

You'll see `(hacklab)` appear at the prompt. That means it's active! Now any `pip install` command will target this environment.

slides.title: Check Which Python You're Using
slides.content: After activation, verify you're in the right place:
slides.codeSnippet:
# Windows
where python

# macOS/Linux
which python

slides.title: PowerShell Execution Policy 🚫
slides.content:
## On Windows PowerShell

If you get an error about scripts being disabled, run:
```
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned
```
Then retry activation. This allows local scripts to run safely.

quizData.question: How do you know a virtual environment is active?

options.text: The terminal prompt shows the environment name in parentheses

quizData.explanation: The prompt changes to show `(env_name)` confirming activation.

slides.title: Installing Packages Inside the Venv
slides.content:
# Now Use pip Safely

With `(hacklab)` active, run:
```
pip install requests
```
This installs the `requests` library **only** inside `hacklab`. Your system Python remains untouched.

slides.title: Deactivating & Cleanup
slides.content:
# Leave the Sandbox

Just type:
```
deactivate
```
The prompt returns to normal. To completely remove the lab, simply **delete the `hacklab` folder** – that's it! No uninstaller needed.

This is why venvs are perfect for hacking: try dangerous libraries, break things, wipe it, and start fresh.

quizData.question: Deleting the virtual environment folder removes all packages installed inside it.
quizData.explanation: Everything is inside that folder. Delete it, and the venv is gone completely.

slides.title: Pro Tip 💡
slides.content:
## Use Descriptive Names

Name your venvs after the project, e.g., `port_scanner_env` or `web_recon_venv`. This makes it clear which environment belongs to which tool.

slides.title: Your First Lab is Ready! 🎉
slides.content:
# Time to Experiment

You now have a safe, isolated Python playground. In the next lesson, we'll master `pip` to load it with hacking libraries.
